title: Stoic in the world
hookLine: the two cities: your town and all humanity

lines: A LOST DOG ON ELM STREET.
cards: Your phone shows you a flood on another continent, a war, an election two oceans away, a famine far away.
Then, in the same scroll, a post from your neighborhood group: someone's lost a dog, the library needs volunteers, the potholes on Elm Street.
Two worlds, one screen, and a pull to care about all of it, with very little anyone can do about most of it. Seneca had an old idea for exactly this: two cities.

teach.b: First, the two cities. Seneca writes that each of us belongs to two commonwealths. One is huge and truly shared, by gods and humans alike, whose borders we measure by the path of the sun.
The other is the one we happened to be born into: Athens, Carthage, or wherever. Some people serve both at once, he says; some only the larger, some only the smaller. Second, Marcus's version.

teach.h: AS ANTONINUS, ROME; AS HUMAN, THE WORLD.
teach.b: As Antoninus, he writes, his city and country is Rome; as a human being, it is the world. The emperor of Rome, reminding himself privately that Rome wasn't the biggest thing he belonged to. Third, the old word.

Diogenes the Cynic, asked where he came from, is said to have answered: I'm a citizen of the world. Kosmopolitēs. The Stoics took up the idea and gave it weight; Marcus calls every human being a fellow citizen.
Fourth, the phone. The world city is too big to carry alone; nobody can fix the flood.

teach.h: ONE REAL THING FOR EACH CITY.
teach.b: But you can do one real thing for it: give, learn, speak up, treat a stranger online as a fellow citizen. And the small city is close enough to touch: the dog, the library, the pothole.
The Stoic in the world doesn't drown in the big city or hide in the small one.
They serve both, a little, on purpose. That turns helpless scrolling back into citizenship.

how: Some Stoic practitioners think of themselves as citizens of both their local community and all humanity, and try to do something concrete for each.

o: the Stoic name for the gods' city among the stars
citizen of the world, Diogenes' answer the Stoics kept
a person loyal to one city above all the others

p: the city you were born into

s: Seneca says we belong to two commonwealths
one vast and shared by all, one assigned by birth.
Marcus thought Rome was the largest thing he belonged to
as a human being, he wrote, his city was the world.
the Stoic citizen of the world ignores their own town
some serve both cities at once; the practice is one thing for each.

games.q: a flood abroad and a lost dog nearby, both on your phone. what does the two-cities idea suggest?
o: only the world matters; ignore the dog
do one real thing for each city
close the app; neither is your business
games.why: Seneca and Marcus both held two citizenships; the practice is to serve both, a little, on purpose.

practice: Picture your small city first, your street, your town, and one face from it, a neighbor or a shopkeeper.
Then let the view widen like a camera pulling back, to your country, the whole planet turning in the sun, and somewhere on it one stranger you'll never meet, living their ordinary day.
Hold both faces, and let one small thing for each city come to mind.

wordCard.voice: Kosmopolitēs, citizen of the world, Diogenes the Cynic's old answer, taken up by the Stoics to mean belonging to all humanity. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: citizen of the world, a word credited to Diogenes the Cynic.

carryVoice: Your line: both cities. The street and the planet both count you as a citizen. See you tomorrow.

sources.work: Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers
